Chapter 7: Family, Forgiveness, and the Long Shadow of the Past
You know, no matter how far we go or how much we change, the past has this uncanny way of tagging along, doesn't it? For Sandra, her path to self-acceptance was always a little haunted by family memories—by parents who just couldn’t see her for who she truly was, siblings who slowly faded away, and children left behind in the messiness of her own survival and transformation.
There were stretches of time when she barely spoke with her family. Maybe an awkward phone call here and there, but mostly, just long, heavy silences. Those old wounds of rejection? They ran deep. And forgiveness... well, it wasn’t something that just happened overnight. Sandra would often find herself wondering—what if things had been different? Was there ever a way to close the gap between who she really was, and who her family expected her to be? That craving for connection, for belonging, it never fully disappeared, even as she built a whole new life for herself.
Every now and then, though, there’d be a flicker of hope. Like the time a hesitant letter arrived from a sibling one spring, kind of testing the waters and opening the door to a careful conversation. Or when one of her children, now grown, reached out with honest questions, trying to understand the choices that shaped their lives. These moments were loaded—with anger, regret, hope, and love all tangled up together. And Sandra realized something big: forgiveness isn’t a one-time thing. It’s a process. It takes patience, and a lot of vulnerability from everyone involved.
Along the way, Sandra discovered that family isn’t just about blood. It’s also about choice. Over the years, she built a new kind of family—friends, colleagues, even clients—people who accepted her just as she was, who showed up with support and without judgment. These relationships became her anchor, her reminder that belonging is possible, even if it looks nothing like she once pictured.
Her work in trauma cleaning put her right in the middle of other families’ crises. She saw up close how grief and loss could drive people apart. Secrets and shame? They could linger for years, poisoning relationships. But even in the middle of heartbreak, Sandra witnessed moments of real grace—siblings coming together to clear out a parent’s home, children forgiving old hurts, strangers reaching out with unexpected comfort. Seeing these moments firsthand taught her that healing is always possible, even for the most fractured families.
When Sandra looks back now, she knows the long shadow of her past will never completely fade. The pain of rejection, that longing to be accepted, the memories of loss—they’re all part of her. But she also sees the distance she’s traveled, and the strength she’s found along the way. Her journey isn’t about erasing the past. It’s about learning to live with it, to find meaning and hope, even when things hurt.
